A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedXpertQA. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 16 models, leakage measurements, inference-time scaling comparisons, and model-error analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds model evaluations, an aggregated human reference baseline, and an expert audit of reasoning labels.

M1.justification: The filtering, augmentation, expert review, and GPT-4o annotation procedures remain the same, including the appendix prompts. Changing 'three' augmentation models to 'two' in the introduction resolves an inconsistency: both versions' Section 3.2 already specifies GPT-4o and Claude. The new label audit validates the existing annotation method.

E1.justification: Both retain the 4,460-question Text/MM benchmark covering 17 specialties, 11 body systems, and three task categories. The human reference reuses source responses already involved in construction. Appendix B.2 discusses cited HLE results without introducing an original HLE evaluation; Appendix F tabulates comparisons already plotted in Figure 1.

E2.justification: v3 Tables 4–5 retain all 16 original models and add o3-mini, LLaMA-3-70B-UltraMedical, and an Expert (Pre-Licensed) human comparator. This extends the existing comparison without replacing its model lineup.

E3.justification: v3 extends the existing 10% sampled evaluation to o3-mini and introduces protocols for aggregating original human responses and auditing annotation labels. Existing model prompting, decoding, and splits remain unchanged. The audit's stated 10% sample conflicts with its counts: 490 Text plus 400 MM questions equal 20% of the test sets.

E4.justification: Section 3.3 adds an expert check of Reasoning/Understanding labels, reporting 28 errors among 490 Text questions and 11 among 400 MM questions. Existing leakage, scaling, body-system, and error analyses remain. Appendix B.1 proposes incomplete-input robustness tests as future work, without reporting such experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The sampling seed remains 42. New human-response counts and annotation-error frequencies do not introduce uncertainty quantification; Appendix B.1 discusses uncertainty estimation only as a future clinical safeguard.

E6.justification: All original model-table scores are unchanged. Added results include o3-mini's sampled Text accuracy of 37.30, human overall accuracy of 43.92, construction-stage counts, and annotation-audit outcomes. UltraMedical's reported average of 21.80 exceeds both subgroup scores, 20.03 and 21.05. The MM image count changes from 2,839 to 2,852 in the comparison table, and Figure 1's o1 gap changes from 50.6 to 51.3.

T1.justification: The Brier-score definition and filtering mathematics remain unchanged. Neither version contains additional theoretical results or proofs, and v3's expanded explanations introduce no new formal reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a difficult, clinically grounded medical benchmark, leakage mitigation, and a reasoning-oriented subset. Updating the evaluation count from 16 to 18 models expands supporting evidence without redefining those claims.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly identifies alignment with U.S. medical practice and adds a substantive distinction between synthetic benchmark performance and clinical readiness in Appendix B.1. It also explains why limited similarity filtering remains useful and argues that original-question human accuracy transfers to augmented questions, although that transfer is not directly tested.

D1.justification: v3 adds construction-stage counts, human-response provenance and coverage, an explicit mention of option shuffling, and a complete worked evaluation example replacing v1's abbreviated example. It adds a leaderboard link and evaluation-only usage instructions. Existing code access, model identifiers, and substantive prompt templates remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for o3-mini, UltraMedical, HLE, and MedReason. New Appendix B.2 positions MedXpertQA against the medical HLE subset using cited findings about difficulty and size. The established related-work framework and earlier benchmark comparisons remain.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized language improvements and expands explanations of construction, annotation, and human comparison. It adds discussion and full-results appendices and relocates the expanded evaluation example. The main section sequence and most existing appendix prose, guidelines, and prompts are preserved.

P2.justification: v3 retains all six numbered figures but redraws Figures 1 and 5, removes Figure 4's panel subtitles, and adjusts captions and placement. It regroups average columns in the main results table, adds comparator rows and two tables, and introduces boxed appendix callouts. The overall document layout remains similar.

improvement.justification: Construction counts, the annotation audit, and clearer applicability limits make v3 more transparent and better qualified while preserving the original evidence. These gains are limited by the audit's inconsistent sample percentage and UltraMedical's impossible reported average. The human baseline adds context, but its comparability remains unverified because it uses responses to original questions before augmentation.
